stops.name: Basra, a night without a lantern, her shining finger
stops.campa: Hasan comes one night with two or three friends to visit Rabia, and finds she has no lantern lit in her hermitage; their hearts yearn for a little light to sit by. Rabia blows upon her own hunger, and from that breath her finger begins to shine like a lamp until dawn, giving the visitors light enough to sit in and talk by. The tradition defends the wonder by the same logic it uses for Moses' luminous hand: whoever walks closely enough in a prophet's footsteps may carry a grain of prophethood, however small, in an otherwise ordinary, famished body.

stops.name: Basra, the wax, the needle, and the hair
stops.campa: Rabia sends Hasan three small objects with no letter of explanation: a piece of wax, a needle, and a hair. The message is meant to be read, not told: be like the wax, which lights the world by consuming itself; be like the needle, always at plain, naked work; and when both of these have been achieved, a thousand years will pass for you as lightly as a single hair. It is teaching reduced to its barest materials, the whole discipline of self-consuming service handed across Basra in a folded scrap of cloth rather than a sermon.
stops.quote: Be like wax. Illumine the world, and yourself burn. Be like a needle, always be working naked. When you have done these two things, a thousand years will be for you as a hair.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the proposal, 'being has disappeared'
stops.campa: Hasan asks Rabia at last whether she desires that they marry. She answers that the tie of marriage binds those who still possess a separate being to bind; in her, being has vanished, she exists only through Him and belongs wholly to Him, and lives in the shadow of His control alone. If Hasan wants her hand, she tells him, he must ask it of God, not of her. Pressed further for the secret of this state, she answers that she lost every 'found' thing in Him, and that where Hasan knows the how of knowing God, she knows only the howless.
stops.quote: The tie of marriage applies to those who have being. Here being has disappeared, for I have become naughted to self and exist only through Him. I belong wholly to Him. I live in the shadow of His control. You must ask my hand of Him, not of me.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the Emir's letter of proposal
stops.campa: Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Hashimi, the Abbasid governor of Basra, sends to Rabia offering marriage, a great dowry, and an income that would end her poverty at a stroke. She answers him in a letter rather than in person, refusing not the man's rank but the whole shape of the offer: it would bring her no happiness, she writes, to have him owned by her or herself occupied by him, kept even for a glance from the one relation she has spent a lifetime narrowing her house to hold. The governor's wealth is declined as firmly as the poorest suitor's onions once were.
stops.quote: It brings me no happiness that you should become my slave, and that I should be owned by you, and that you should keep me occupied, away from Allah, even for a glance.
stops.quote_source: Sufi hagiographic tradition (Ibn Khallikan; Jami, Nafahat al-Uns; popularized in Margaret Smith, Rabi'a the Mystic, 1928)

stops.name: Basra, the household of women, Maryam and 'Abda
stops.campa: Around Rabia's hermitage a small household of women gathers who will not be sent home like the suitors. Maryam of Basra stands the whole night in ecstatic worship beside her, given to repeating God's own tenderness toward His servants until dawn finds her still standing. 'Abda bint Abi Shawwal binds herself to Rabia's service as her devoted attendant, present at the prayer vigils and, later, at the deathbed itself. Where the men of Basra bring proposals and purses, these women bring only their company, and it is this company, not any suitor's offer, that Rabia keeps.

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, the illness that followed a vision of Paradise
stops.campa: Rabia falls gravely sick, and those around her ask the cause. She answers that she gazed upon Paradise, and her Lord disciplined her for the gazing, as though the reward itself were a distraction requiring correction. The illness settles over the hermitage that had until now been the scene mostly of small wonders and sharp sayings; now it becomes the site of a long dying, visited over the years by the same generation of Basra's ascetics who have argued with her, tested her, and loved her, come now to sit at the pillow of the woman who refused them all.
stops.quote: I gazed upon Paradise, and my Lord disciplined me.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, her door, the notable's purse of gold
stops.campa: Hasan comes to visit the sick Rabia and finds at her hermitage door one of Basra's notables, weeping, holding out a purse of gold for her care and afraid she will refuse it. He asks Hasan to intercede for him. Rabia, told of the gift, answers that God provides for those who insult Him, so surely He provides for those who love Him; she does not know whether any man's wealth is lawfully come by, and cannot take what she cannot vouch for. She recalls mending a torn shirt once by lamplight and tearing the stitches out again rather than let the memory of that borrowed light trouble her heart.
stops.quote: He provides for those who insult Him, and shall He not provide for those who love Him? Ever since I knew Him, I have turned my back upon His creatures. I know not whether any man's property is lawful or not; how then can I take it?
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, Sofyan al-Thawri and twelve years of dates
stops.campa: Abd al-Wahed-e Amer comes with Sofyan al-Thawri to visit the sick Rabia, too awed to speak first. Sofyan tells her to pray for ease from her pain; she asks whether it was not God who willed her to suffer it, and if so how Sofyan can bid her ask the contrary of His own will. Pressed for what she does desire, she confesses that for twelve years she has wanted fresh dates, cheap and common as they are in Basra, and has never once eaten one, since a servant of God has no business desiring anything her Lord has not Himself already given.
stops.quote: By the glory of God, for twelve years now I have been desiring fresh dates. You know that in Basra dates are of no consequence. Yet till now I have not eaten any; for I am His servant, and what business has a servant to desire?
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, Malik ibn Dinar and the broken pitcher
stops.campa: Malik ibn Dinar visits the sick Rabia and finds her whole estate: a broken pitcher she drinks and makes her ablutions from, an old reed mat, and a brick she sometimes uses as a pillow. Grieved, he offers to bring her something from his own rich friends. She rebukes him for the offer as a grievous error: is not her Provider the same as theirs? Has the Provider of the poor ever forgotten them for their poverty, or remembered the rich only for their riches? Since God already knows her estate exactly, she asks, what business has she reminding Him of it through Malik's friends.
stops.quote: Malek, you have committed a grievous error. Is not my Provider and theirs one and the same?... Since He knows my estate, how should I remind Him? Such is His will, and I too wish as He wills.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, Hasan, Malik, and Shaqiq on the lash of the Lord
stops.campa: Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, and Shaqiq of Balkh come together to the sick Rabia and each offers a definition of true faith under suffering. Hasan says none is truthful who does not bear the Lord's lash with fortitude; Rabia calls it egoism. Shaqiq says none is truthful who is not grateful for the lash; she says they need better still. Malik says none is truthful who does not delight in the lash; still not enough, she answers. Pressed to better them herself, she pronounces that none is truthful who does not forget the lash entirely in contemplation of the One who deals it.
stops.quote: He is not truthful in his claim who does not forget the lash in contemplation of his Master.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the sickbed, the scholar who reviled the world
stops.campa: A leading scholar of Basra sits beside Rabia's pillow on her sickbed and spends his visit disparaging the world at length, its vanity, its snares, its worthlessness. Rabia tells him plainly that he loves the world very dearly, for it is always the purchaser who disparages the wares he means to bargain down, and a man truly finished with the world would not trouble to mention it at all, for good or ill. As the proverb runs, she says, whoever loves a thing speaks of it often; his lengthy contempt for the world is itself the clearest proof of how much he still wants it.
stops.quote: You love the world very dearly. If you did not love the world, you would not make mention of it so much. It is always the purchaser who disparages the wares.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the hermitage, the death of Rabia
stops.campa: When the hour comes for Rabia to die, those attending her, 'Abda among them, are asked to leave the room, and the door is closed behind them. Some time passes with no sound from within. Then a voice is heard from inside, saying: O soul at peace, return unto thy Lord, well pleased! When those outside open the door at last, they find that she has given up the ghost, alone with the voice that called her, exactly as she has spent every year since the lantern over her head asking to be alone with nothing else.
stops.quote: O soul at peace, return unto thy Lord, well-pleased!
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry (echoing Qur'an 89:27-28)
